The Pre-Launch Website Checklist for Contractors

Complete website launch checklist for contractors. Includes technical, content, SEO, and launch day items. Download the free PDF.

You are about to launch a new contractor website. You have spent weeks (maybe months) on design, copy, and functionality. But one broken form, one missing meta description, or one slow-loading page can turn that launch from a revenue driver into a credibility killer. This is the website launch checklist we use at OnwardCraft before every contractor site goes live. It covers technical validation, content review, SEO setup, and launch day execution. Follow it step by step, and you will not miss a thing.

Why Most Contractor Website Launches Underperform (And How This Checklist Fixes It)

Here is a number that should stop you in your tracks: 88% of online consumers are less likely to return to a site after a bad experience, according to a study by Gomez and Akamai. For contractors, that stat is even more punishing. You do not get repeat visits from homeowners the way an e-commerce store might. You get one shot to make a first impression, and if your site fails on launch day, that homeowner calls your competitor instead.

The problem is not that contractors do not care about their websites. The problem is that launching a site involves dozens of moving parts, spread across technical infrastructure, content quality, search engine optimization, and user experience. Most contractors (and even many web designers) rely on memory or informal processes. They forget to test the contact form. They skip mobile responsiveness checks. They launch with placeholder text still on the homepage. These are not small oversights. They are revenue-destroying mistakes.

The Real Cost of a Botched Website Launch

A plumbing contractor in Dallas we worked with last year spent $8,000 on a new site. The design looked great. The copy was solid. But on launch day, the phone number in the header linked to an old disconnected line. For three weeks, no one noticed. By the time they caught it, they had lost an estimated 47 qualified leads. At their average job value of $1,200, that is $56,400 in lost revenue from one broken phone link.

This is not an isolated story. We see versions of it constantly. An HVAC company in Phoenix launched a site where the "Request a Quote" button submitted to a dead email address. A roofing contractor in Atlanta forgot to set up SSL, so Google flagged the site as "Not Secure" and traffic dropped 60% in the first month. A landscaping business in Denver had beautiful portfolio images that took 8 seconds to load on mobile, and their bounce rate hit 78%.

Every one of these failures was preventable. Every one would have been caught by a rigorous website pre-launch checklist. That is what this article gives you. Not a vague list of "best practices." A step-by-step, contractor-specific website go-live checklist that you can work through systematically.

What Makes This Checklist Different

Most website launch checklists you will find online are written for generic businesses or SaaS companies. They tell you to "check your analytics" and "test your forms" without explaining what "test" actually means. They do not account for the specific challenges contractors face: local SEO dominance, emergency service calls, service area pages, before-and-after galleries, license and insurance verification, and the intense competition in home services markets.

This checklist is built from 200+ contractor website launches. It is designed for roofers, plumbers, electricians, HVAC technicians, landscapers, painters, remodelers, and every other trade that serves homeowners. It prioritizes the items that actually move the needle for contractor lead generation. It skips the generic advice and focuses on what makes a contractor website convert visitors into booked appointments.

Short answer: A contractor website launch checklist is a systematic validation process covering technical functionality, content accuracy, SEO setup, and launch day execution. It prevents broken features, missed leads, and search engine penalties that cost contractors tens of thousands in lost revenue.

Technical Checklist: The Foundation That Everything Else Builds On

If your website's technical foundation is cracked, no amount of great copy or beautiful design will save it. This section covers the technical validation steps that must happen before any contractor site goes live. Skip these, and you are building on sand.

Domain and Hosting Verification

Start with the basics that are shockingly easy to mess up. Verify that your domain is properly registered and not expiring within the next 12 months. We have seen contractors launch a site on a domain that expires in 30 days, then forget to renew it. Set auto-renewal on. Confirm the domain registrar account is accessible and the contact email is current.

Check your hosting setup. For contractor sites, we recommend hosting with an uptime guarantee of 99.9% or higher. Shared hosting is fine for brochure sites, but if you are running appointment scheduling, live chat, or portfolio galleries with hundreds of images, consider managed WordPress hosting or a VPS. Test your hosting's server response time using tools like GTmetrix or Pingdom. Anything over 800ms is a problem.

Verify your SSL certificate is installed and working correctly. Every page should load over HTTPS, not HTTP. Check for mixed content warnings (when an HTTPS page loads HTTP resources). Browsers flag these aggressively now, and they kill trust instantly. A homeowner seeing "Not Secure" next to your URL will back out before they even see your hero section.

Cross-Browser and Cross-Device Testing

Your new website checklist must include real device testing, not just resizing your browser window. Test on actual iPhones, Android devices, iPads, and desktop computers. Check Safari, Chrome, Firefox, and Edge. Each browser renders CSS differently, and contractor sites often use complex layouts for service grids, testimonial carousels, and before/after sliders that break in unexpected ways.

Pay special attention to your navigation menu on mobile. The "hamburger" menu should open smoothly, links should be large enough to tap without zooming, and dropdowns should not require precision finger-work. We recommend a minimum tap target size of 48x48 pixels for all interactive elements.

Test your forms on mobile specifically. Typing into form fields on a phone is already annoying. If your fields are too small, if the keyboard covers the submit button, or if the form does not scroll properly, your mobile conversion rate will crater. According to Google, 61% of users will not return to a mobile site they had trouble accessing.

Form and Conversion Path Testing

This is where most contractor website launches fail. Every form on your site needs rigorous testing. That means:

  1. Fill out every form completely and submit it. Confirm the submission reaches the correct email address or CRM.
  2. Test form validation. Submit with empty required fields, invalid email formats, and phone numbers with too few digits. Error messages should be clear and helpful.
  3. Test the "thank you" page or confirmation message. Users need immediate feedback that their submission worked.
  4. Test file upload fields if you have them (common for "send us photos of your project" forms).
  5. Test autoresponder emails. If someone fills out your contact form at 2 AM, do they get an immediate "we received your message" email?

Test every conversion path, not just contact forms. Click your phone number on mobile. Does it trigger a call? Click your email address. Does it open the user's email client with a pre-filled subject line? Test your "Get a Quote" buttons, your "Schedule Now" links, and any third-party booking integrations.

Site Speed and Performance

Page speed is a ranking factor for Google, and it is a conversion factor for every visitor. According to Portent, a site that loads in 1 second has a 3x higher conversion rate than a site that loads in 5 seconds. For contractors, where visitors are often in emergency mode ("my AC just died and it is 95 degrees"), speed is even more critical.

Load Time Bounce Rate Impact Conversion Rate
1 second Baseline Highest
3 seconds +32% -20%
5 seconds +90% -38%
10 seconds +123% -70%

Run your site through Google PageSpeed Insights. Aim for a score of 80+ on mobile and 90+ on desktop. Compress all images using tools like TinyPNG or ShortPixel. Enable browser caching. Minify CSS and JavaScript files. If you are using a page builder like Elementor or Divi, be aware that they add significant bloat. Consider whether the design flexibility is worth the speed penalty.

Security and Backup Setup

Before launch, install a security plugin or configure server-level security. Set up a Web Application Firewall (WAF) if your host provides one. Change default login URLs. Enforce strong passwords for all user accounts. Limit login attempts to prevent brute force attacks.

Set up automated backups. Daily backups are ideal, weekly is the minimum. Store backups off-site (not on the same server as your website). Test restoring from a backup before launch. We have seen contractors discover their backup system was broken only after they needed it.

Short answer: Technical validation for a contractor website launch includes domain/hosting verification, SSL installation, cross-browser testing on real devices, form submission testing across all conversion paths, PageSpeed optimization targeting 80+ mobile scores, and automated backup configuration.

Content Checklist: Every Word, Image, and Page Must Pull Its Weight

Technical perfection means nothing if your content is weak. Homeowners visiting contractor websites are making high-stakes decisions. They are inviting strangers into their homes. They are spending thousands of dollars. Your content must build trust, demonstrate expertise, and make the next step obvious.

Homepage Content Validation

Your homepage has about 3 seconds to answer three questions: What do you do? Who do you serve? Why should I trust you? Check that your headline clearly states your primary service and service area. "Denver's Most Trusted Roofing Contractor" is better than "Welcome to Our Website."

Verify your homepage includes these trust signals above the fold: your phone number (clickable on mobile), your service area, years in business, and a key differentiator. A photo of the owner or team adds human connection that stock photos cannot replicate. According to a study by Nielsen Norman Group, photos of real people increase perceived trustworthiness significantly compared to generic imagery.

Check for placeholder text. Search your entire site for "Lorem ipsum," "Sample text," "Coming soon," or any other filler content. These are embarrassingly common on launched sites. Use your browser's find function (Ctrl+F or Cmd+F) to search for these terms across every page.

Service Page Completeness

Every service you offer needs its own dedicated page. Not a bullet point on a general services page. A full page with unique content, specific to that service. This matters for SEO (Google ranks specific pages for specific queries) and for conversion (homeowners want to know you specialize in their exact problem).

Each service page should include: a clear description of the service, the problems it solves, your process, what makes your approach different, FAQs specific to that service, and a strong call-to-action. A plumbing contractor should have separate pages for emergency plumbing, drain cleaning, water heater repair, pipe replacement, and fixture installation. Each page should target different keywords and address different homeowner concerns.

Check that service pages do not duplicate content. If your "Roof Repair" and "Roof Replacement" pages have identical introductory paragraphs, Google will likely ignore one of them. Write unique content for every page, even when the services are similar.

About Page and Team Information

The About page is often the second-most visited page on contractor websites. Homeowners want to know who they are hiring. Verify your About page includes: your company story, your mission or values, team photos with names and roles, licensing and insurance information, and any certifications or affiliations (BBB, Angi, local chamber of commerce).

Include your license numbers if required by your state. Some states mandate that contractors display license numbers on their websites. Even where it is not required, transparency about licensing builds trust. Homeowners know that licensed contractors can be held accountable.

Portfolio and Project Galleries

Before-and-after photos are conversion gold for contractors. But they must be done right. Check that every image loads properly and has alt text describing the project. "Bathroom remodel in Phoenix with walk-in shower and quartz countertops" is better than "IMG_4523.jpg."

Organize galleries by service type. A kitchen remodeling contractor should have separate galleries for kitchen remodels, bathroom remodels, and whole-home renovations. Include project details: location, timeline, materials used, and any challenges overcome. This demonstrates expertise and helps visitors imagine their own project.

Optimize all images for web. A before-and-after slider with 20MB images will destroy your page speed. Compress images to under 200KB each without visible quality loss. Use WebP format where possible. Lazy-load images that are below the fold.

Testimonials and Reviews Integration

Social proof is critical for contractor websites. According to BrightLocal, 87% of consumers read online reviews for local businesses. Your website should feature testimonials prominently, but they must be credible.

Verify that testimonials include: the customer's full name (not "John D."), their location, the service they received, and ideally a photo. Video testimonials are even more powerful. Check that all testimonials are real and that you have permission to use them. Fake testimonials are not just unethical, they are illegal under FTC guidelines.

If you integrate reviews from Google, Yelp, or Facebook, ensure the integration is working and displays current reviews. A widget showing reviews from 2019 looks worse than no reviews at all.

Contact Information and Service Area Clarity

Every page should make it easy to contact you. Check that your phone number is in the header, footer, and multiple places within the content. Your physical address (or addresses) should be on the contact page and footer. If you serve multiple cities, list them clearly.

Be specific about your service area. "We serve the greater metro area" is vague. "We serve Phoenix, Scottsdale, Tempe, Mesa, Gilbert, and Chandler" is specific and helps with local SEO. Consider creating individual service area pages for each major city you serve. A roofing contractor in Dallas should have separate pages for Dallas, Plano, Frisco, and McKinney roofing services.

Short answer: Content validation for a contractor website includes verifying homepage clarity, creating dedicated pages for every service with unique copy, building a trust-focused About page, optimizing portfolio images with descriptive alt text, featuring credible testimonials with full names, and clearly defining your service area on every relevant page.

SEO Checklist: Setting Up Your Site to Rank Before It Goes Live

SEO is not something you bolt on after launch. The foundation must be built correctly from day one. Getting it wrong means months of lost rankings while Google figures out (or fails to figure out) what your site is about. For contractors competing in local markets, early SEO mistakes can cede valuable positions to competitors.

Keyword Research and On-Page Optimization

Every page should target a specific primary keyword. Your homepage targets your broadest term ("roofing contractor Dallas"). Service pages target specific services ("emergency roof repair Dallas"). Blog posts target informational queries ("how long does a roof replacement take").

Verify that each page includes the primary keyword in: the title tag (under 60 characters), the meta description (under 160 characters), the H1 heading, the first paragraph, at least one H2 subheading, the URL slug, and image alt text. Do not stuff keywords unnaturally. Google's natural language processing is sophisticated enough to understand context and synonyms.

Check for duplicate title tags and meta descriptions. Every page should have unique metadata. Use a tool like Screaming Frog (free for up to 500 URLs) to crawl your site and identify duplicates, missing tags, and tags that are too long.

Local SEO Setup

For contractors, local SEO is everything. Homeowners search for services near them. If you are not optimized for local search, you are invisible to your best prospects.

First, verify your Google Business Profile is claimed, verified, and optimized. It should match your website's name, address, and phone number exactly. Any discrepancy ("St." vs "Street," different phone numbers, suite numbers formatted differently) confuses Google and hurts rankings.

Implement LocalBusiness schema markup on your site. This structured data tells Google your business name, address, phone number, hours, service area, and services offered. Use JSON-LD format and validate it with Google's Rich Results Test tool.

Build location pages for each city you serve. Each page should have unique content about that specific area. Mention local landmarks, neighborhood names, and area-specific concerns ("homes in this area often face hail damage from spring storms"). Do not create thin pages that just swap out the city name. Google penalizes doorway pages.

Technical SEO Foundations

Submit your XML sitemap to Google Search Console before launch. If your site is replacing an old site, set up 301 redirects from every old URL to the most relevant new URL. Failing to redirect old pages destroys your existing rankings and creates broken backlinks.

Check your robots.txt file. Make sure it is not blocking important pages. Make sure your staging site is either password-protected or blocked from indexing. We have seen contractors accidentally launch with their staging site indexed, creating duplicate content issues that took months to resolve.

Verify your site has a proper canonical tag on every page. This prevents duplicate content issues when the same content is accessible via multiple URLs (with and without "www," with and without trailing slashes, with URL parameters).

Internal Linking Structure

Internal links help Google discover your pages and understand your site structure. They also distribute "link equity" (ranking power) throughout your site. Check that:

  • Every page is reachable within 3 clicks from the homepage
  • Your most important pages (top services) have the most internal links pointing to them
  • Navigation menus are logical and consistent across all pages
  • Footer links include key service pages and location pages
  • Breadcrumb navigation is implemented for deep pages

Use descriptive anchor text for internal links. "Learn about our emergency plumbing services" is better than "Click here." Descriptive anchor text helps both users and search engines understand what the linked page is about.

Image Optimization for Search

Contractor websites are image-heavy. Portfolio photos, team photos, equipment photos, before-and-after comparisons. Every image is an SEO opportunity.

Rename image files before uploading. "emergency-plumber-fixing-burst-pipe-dallas.jpg" is better than "IMG_2345.jpg." Write descriptive alt text for every image. Alt text serves two purposes: it makes your site accessible to visually impaired users, and it gives Google context about the image content.

Compress images without visible quality loss. Use responsive images that serve different sizes for different devices. Implement lazy loading so images below the fold do not slow down initial page load. Consider using a CDN for image delivery if you have a large portfolio.

Short answer: SEO setup before launch includes unique title tags and meta descriptions for every page, claimed and optimized Google Business Profile, LocalBusiness schema markup, 301 redirects from old URLs, XML sitemap submission, logical internal linking within 3 clicks from homepage, and fully optimized images with descriptive filenames and alt text.

Launch Day Checklist: Executing the Go-Live Without Drama

Launch day is not the time for improvisation. Every step should be planned, every contingency considered. This section covers the exact sequence we follow when taking a contractor website live.

Pre-Launch Final Review (T-24 Hours)

Twenty-four hours before launch, run a complete site crawl using Screaming Frog or Sitebulb. Export a list of all URLs, status codes, title tags, meta descriptions, and H1s. Review this spreadsheet for errors. Look for 404s, redirect chains, duplicate titles, missing meta descriptions, and pages with no H1.

Test every form one final time. Send test submissions from different devices and browsers. Confirm emails are received. Confirm CRM integrations are working. Confirm autoresponders are sending.

Review every page for spelling and grammar errors. Read copy aloud. Errors that your eyes skip over silently become obvious when spoken. Consider using a tool like Grammarly, but do not rely on it exclusively. It misses context-specific errors.

The Launch Sequence

When it is time to go live, follow this exact order:

  1. Put up a maintenance page if your site is currently receiving traffic
  2. Point the domain to the new hosting/server (update DNS records)
  3. Wait for DNS propagation (can take minutes to 48 hours, usually under 2 hours)
  4. Remove any noindex tags or robots.txt blocks that prevented indexing during development
  5. Verify the SSL certificate is working on the live domain
  6. Test the homepage loads correctly
  7. Test 5-10 key internal pages
  8. Test all forms on the live domain
  9. Submit the XML sitemap to Google Search Console
  10. Submit the site for indexing via Search Console's URL Inspection tool

Do not skip the noindex removal step. We have seen multiple contractors launch sites that remain invisible to Google for weeks because the development team forgot to remove noindex tags. Check your source code for <meta name="robots" content="noindex"> on every page.

Post-Launch Validation (First 48 Hours)

The first 48 hours after launch are critical. Monitor Google Search Console daily for crawl errors, indexing issues, and mobile usability problems. Check Google Analytics (or your preferred analytics platform) to confirm tracking is working and data is flowing.

Test your site speed on the live server. Hosting environments often perform differently than staging environments. A site that loaded in 2 seconds on staging might take 5 seconds on the production server if the hosting plan is underpowered.

Check for broken links using a tool like Broken Link Checker. New sites often have placeholder links, internal links pointing to staging URLs, or external links that were copied from templates. Fix every 404 immediately.

Monitor contact form submissions closely. If submission volume drops unexpectedly, something broke. If you receive a flood of spam, your form protection (CAPTCHA, honeypot) is not working.

Common Launch Day Mistakes to Avoid

After 200+ launches, we have seen the same mistakes repeatedly. Here is what to watch for:

  • Forgetting to update email addresses: Contact forms still sending to the web developer's test email
  • Broken phone links: Click-to-call links with typos in the tel: protocol
  • Staging URLs in content: Links or images still pointing to staging.yoursite.com
  • Missing analytics: Google Analytics or Google Tag Manager code not installed on the live site
  • Wrong business hours: Copy-pasted from a template and not updated
  • Outdated copyright dates: Still showing last year (or worse, a template's placeholder year)
  • Social media links pointing to templates: Facebook links going to facebook.com/template-page

Short answer: Launch day execution involves a final 24-hour crawl and review, sequential DNS propagation and noindex removal, immediate sitemap submission to Google Search Console, and intensive 48-hour monitoring for crawl errors, broken links, form failures, and analytics tracking issues.

FAQ: Real Questions Contractors Ask About Website Launches

These are the questions we hear most often from contractors preparing to launch new websites. The answers are based on real launches, real problems, and real solutions.

How long does a contractor website launch typically take?

A well-prepared launch takes 2-4 hours of active work, plus 24-48 hours of monitoring. DNS propagation is usually the longest variable. If you are switching hosting providers, plan for up to 48 hours for full global propagation. The actual site deployment (uploading files, updating databases, configuring settings) takes 1-2 hours for most contractor sites. Rushing the process increases error risk significantly.

Should I launch on a specific day of the week?

Launch on Tuesday, Wednesday, or Thursday during business hours. Avoid Monday (you are catching up from the weekend), Friday (you have less support availability if issues arise), and weekends (your web developer may not be available). Launching mid-week gives you two full business days to identify and fix issues before the weekend.

What is the most commonly missed item on a website pre-launch checklist?

Form testing. We estimate 30-40% of contractor websites launch with at least one broken form, incorrect email routing, or missing autoresponder. The second most missed item is removing noindex tags from staging. The third is updating contact information copied from templates.

How do I know if my new website is ready to launch?

Your site is ready when: every page loads without errors on desktop and mobile, every form submits correctly to the right destination, every link works, every image displays, page speed scores are 80+ on mobile, all content is final with no placeholders, SEO metadata is complete and unique, and you have tested the entire site on at least one real phone and one real computer.

Do I need to tell Google when I launch a new website?

Yes. Submit your XML sitemap through Google Search Console immediately after launch. Use the URL Inspection tool to request indexing for your homepage and key pages. If you are replacing an existing site, submit a change of address request in Search Console. If you have a new domain, expect 2-8 weeks for Google to fully crawl and index your site.

What should I do with my old website when launching a new one?

Set up 301 redirects from every old URL to the most relevant new URL. Do not redirect everything to the homepage. A page about "emergency plumbing" on the old site should redirect to the emergency plumbing page on the new site. Keep the old hosting active for 30-60 days to ensure all redirects are working. After that period, you can cancel the old hosting.

How soon after launch will my contractor website start ranking?

New domains typically take 3-6 months to rank for competitive local keywords. Established domains with proper redirects may see rankings transfer within 2-4 weeks. If you are in a less competitive market or targeting long-tail keywords ("emergency tankless water heater repair Scottsdale"), you might see rankings within weeks. Consistent content publishing and link building accelerate the timeline.

What happens if I find a mistake after launch?

Fix it immediately. There is no "grace period" where visitors forgive errors. A broken contact form costs you leads from day one. A misspelled headline damages credibility instantly. The good news is that most post-launch fixes are quick. The key is having a monitoring process that catches issues fast. Check your site daily for the first two weeks, then weekly for the first month.

Should I announce my website launch on social media?

Yes, but wait 48-72 hours after launch. This gives you time to catch and fix any issues before driving traffic. Announce on Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, and any other platforms where your customers are active. Include a specific call-to-action: "Book a free estimate through our new site" rather than just "Check out our new website." Consider running a small launch promotion (10% off for online bookings) to drive initial traffic and conversions.

How much should a contractor budget for ongoing website maintenance?

Budget $100-300 per month for basic maintenance (updates, backups, security monitoring). Budget $500-1,500 per month if you are investing in ongoing SEO, content creation, and conversion optimization. A website is not a "set it and forget it" asset. WordPress core updates, plugin updates, security patches, content refreshes, and performance monitoring are ongoing requirements. Sites that are not maintained become slow, insecure, and outdated within 12-18 months.

Can I launch a website myself, or do I need a professional?

Technically capable contractors can handle simple launches, especially if using a hosted platform like Wix or Squarespace. However, WordPress launches involve more complexity (hosting configuration, plugin management, database setup, security hardening). For contractors whose website is a primary lead source, professional launch management is worth the investment. One missed redirect or broken form costs more than professional launch support.

What is the difference between soft launch and hard launch?

A soft launch means the site is live but you are not actively promoting it yet. You are testing with a small audience, monitoring for issues, and making adjustments. A hard launch means you are actively driving traffic through advertising, email announcements, and social media. We recommend a 48-72 hour soft launch period for all contractor websites. This catches issues before they reach your full audience.

How do I track whether my website launch was successful?

Define success metrics before launch. Common metrics for contractor sites: contact form submissions (target: match or exceed old site within 30 days), phone calls from the website (use call tracking numbers), organic traffic growth (target: 10-20% increase month-over-month for new sites), page speed scores, and search ranking positions for target keywords. Set up Google Analytics goals and Google Search Console before launch so you have baseline data.

Should I keep my old domain or switch to a new one?

Keep your old domain unless you have a compelling reason to switch (rebranding, legal issues, extremely poor domain history). Established domains have built-up authority, backlinks, and recognition. Switching domains means starting your SEO from scratch. If you must switch, plan for a 6-12 month recovery period and invest heavily in redirect management and authority building.

What security measures should be in place before launch?

Minimum security for contractor sites: SSL certificate (HTTPS), strong passwords on all accounts, limited login attempts, regular automated backups stored off-site, security plugin or WAF, and software update plan. If you collect payments online, you need PCI compliance measures. If you store customer data, you need encryption and access controls. Security is not optional. A hacked contractor site damages reputation and can expose customer information.

Conclusion: Launch With Confidence, Not Hope

A website launch is not a single moment. It is a process that starts weeks before go-live day and continues for months after. The contractors who win online are not the ones with the flashiest designs or the biggest budgets. They are the ones who treat their website launch with the same rigor they bring to a job site.

You would not install a water heater without checking every connection. You would not finish a roof without inspecting every shingle. Apply that same standard to your website. Work through the technical checklist. Validate every piece of content. Set up your SEO foundation correctly. Execute your launch day sequence methodically. Monitor relentlessly in the weeks that follow.
